correctness.rationale: The normalized affine interpolation of two nonantipodal points on the round sphere has the same trace as the minimizing great-circle arc. Projection to a fixed coordinate plane gives a segment joining two nonopposite planar rays; its azimuth traces their shorter circular arc independently of latitude or dimension. For independent uniform azimuths on E, different components never survive and a pair in one component of angular length l survives precisely when its coordinate gap does not exceed pi. The two excluded triangular corners of the parameter square have total area (l-pi)_+^2. Summing with weights (l/theta)^2 gives the exact formula. The function f(l)=l^2-(l-pi)_+^2 is convex and has f(l)/l strictly increasing on (0,2pi]; Jensen proves the unique k-equal lower optimizer and strict superadditivity the unattained upper supremum. The single-meridian case is l=theta=2pi and yields 3/4; equal k-component cuts yield 1/k. Exceptional antipodal, opposite-azimuth, and axial points have probability zero under the stated measures. The standalone checker directly interpolates sampled sphere points and tests 225000 cases in dimensions 2,3,5,6, with agreement at tolerance 0.012.

value.rationale: The problem quantifies a geometric connectivity statistic that depends on whether a random shortest ambient geodesic stays within a domain, rather than merely whether endpoints lie inside it. Deleted zero-area meridians alter this probability discontinuously, giving an instructive contrast with area-invariant statistics; the exact all-dimensional classification makes this nonlocal effect measurable. The best/worst arrangement for a fixed angular budget and number of components is solved sharply, including uniqueness and the unattained supremum, and the result applies to all sphere dimensions and latitude sampling laws with uniform azimuth. This is a complete structural family, not a single numerical example or a routine restatement of spherical convexity.
